What is the difference between activated charcoal water filters and carbon filters, which is better?

as far as I know, they are the same, and function well because they have an extremely high surface area, and they adsorb organic molecules which tend to be most related to off smells/off tastes.

I don't suspect they remove ions much, but thats what ion exchange resins are for.

Carbon is an element, Charcoal is a pyrolyzed wood product that is mostly carbon, activated charcoal is just very porous providing lots of surface area and making an excellent filter. "Carbon" is found naturally as diamond, coal, graphite and other minerals and does not have any particular filtering properties. Pyrolysis is thermal decomposition without oxidation/burning. Pyrolyzing wood leaves a highly porous highly carbonaceous structure with lots of open bonding sites that will adsorb most organic and many inorganic compounds, making an excellent filter. To be clear it does not work like a molecular sieve, it sieves out larger particulate by the physical nature of the filter, but it filters smaller and dissolved pollutants as well by chemical bonding. This is also why the filter needs to be changed, as the surface area gets 'used up' and saturated with adsorbed pollutants.

Carbon is a misnomer, charcoal is mostly carbon but also contains some hydrogen and oxygen. It is an industrial product and not a natural mineral of carbon. Activated Charcoal just means charcoal that is suitable for filtering applications (mostly just a certain level of porosity).
